subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: Kashish beti, you think you're the first wife to eat dinner alone? Sit with your Yamini Dadi a minute. When I was twenty-four, your Dada worked nights at the steel plant. For months I kept his plate covered and ate with only the radio for company. On Diwali he slept through the lamps, and I sulked for two days. He came home grey with tiredness and said sorry so often it stopped meaning anything. Then one morning, instead of sulking, I sat him down with his tea. On the back of the calendar we wrote a promise: Sunday lunch together, no matter what. I hung a thick curtain and told the children, 'Papa's sleeping, play in the courtyard.' And he told me honestly when he was too tired to talk. That is how we stayed friends.

qa.q: What promise did Yamini and Dada write on the back of the calendar?
qa.a: Sunday lunch together, no matter what.

qa.q: How did young Yamini feel when Dada slept through Diwali?
qa.a: She felt neglected and hurt, and she sulked for two days.

qa.q: What was the turning point in those night-shift years?
qa.a: The morning Yamini sat Dada down over tea instead of sulking, and they planned shared time, a quiet house for his sleep and honest talk.

qa.q: How did Dada seem to feel about missing family life?
qa.a: He seemed guilty and worn out, coming home grey with tiredness and apologising so often that the word lost its meaning.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a wife who feels neglected as a shift worker misses meals and festivals, his guilt and tiredness, and how planned shared time, quiet for sleep and open talk held them together.

subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: Keerthana worked from home, taking customer calls in the only room of the flat she shared with her sister Trisha. Trisha, a nurse, had been on nights for weeks, sleeping through the day behind a bedsheet hung from the ceiling. Keerthana whispered into her headset for hours and felt like a ghost in her own home. Then Trisha slept through Keerthana's birthday dinner. 'You're never here, even when you're here,' Keerthana said that night. Trisha's eyes filled. 'I know. I hate it too.' They couldn't afford a bigger place. So they made a plan: Keerthana would take morning calls from the building's quiet reading room, Trisha would set an alarm for Sundays, and every Sunday they'd eat breakfast together before Trisha slept. The first Sunday they made dosas and talked until the sun was high.

qa.q: Where did Trisha sleep in the flat?
qa.a: Behind a bedsheet hung from the ceiling.

qa.q: How was Keerthana feeling when she said, 'You're never here, even when you're here'?
qa.a: She felt lonely and neglected, like a ghost whispering all day in her own home.

qa.q: What made their plan work despite the small flat and little money?
qa.a: They talked openly first, then shared the load: morning calls from the reading room, a Sunday alarm and a fixed breakfast together.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel about missing the birthday dinner?
qa.a: Trisha felt guilty and sad; her eyes filled and she admitted she hated it too.

grounding: Shows a sister feeling neglected by a shift worker who feels guilty, and how shared time, quiet for sleep and open talk hold them together despite a small flat.

subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: People ask me, 'Bhupen, how do you two manage?' Honestly, the first year, we didn't. Farida started night duty in the ICU six months after our wedding. I'd cook, eat alone and go to bed beside an empty pillow. When she came home at eight, I was leaving for the office. My cousin's engagement, my father's birthday: she missed both, and I sulked. She'd cry that she was always letting everyone down, and she looked so tired. One Sunday we finally talked properly. Now her roster goes on the fridge, and her off-day breakfast is sacred. I oil the door hinges and take calls on the balcony so she can sleep. We still miss things, but we don't miss each other.

qa.q: What does Bhupen do so that Farida can sleep?
qa.a: Bhupen oils the door hinges and takes calls on the balcony.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel during that first year?
qa.a: Bhupen felt lonely and neglected, eating alone and sulking when Farida missed family events.

qa.q: What helped Bhupen and Farida hold together?
qa.a: An honest talk, the roster on the fridge, a protected off-day breakfast and a quiet house for Farida's sleep.

qa.q: How did Farida experience those missed events?
qa.a: She felt guilty and worn out, crying that she was always letting everyone down.

grounding: The spouse of a night-shift nurse feels neglected, the worker feels guilty, and planning, quiet and talk keep them close.

subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage:
Sunday: Jasleen set plates for lunch with Zubin's parents. Zubin, back from a night driving the goods train, slept through it. His mother sighed, 'Again?' Jasleen smiled for her, then cried quietly while washing up. That evening Zubin woke, saw her face and said, 'I'm sorry. I'm always sorry.' He looked grey.
Wednesday: They sat on the steps with chai and his duty chart and circled two meals a week they could share. Jasleen hung a heavy curtain and asked the neighbours' children to play farther down the lane in the mornings.
Next Sunday: Lunch became dinner at seven. Zubin was awake, rested, and teasing his mother about her pickle.

qa.q: What time was the Sunday meal moved to?
qa.a: Dinner at seven.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel on the first Sunday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and alone, smiling for Zubin's mother but crying quietly while washing up.

qa.q: What did the couple plan on Wednesday?
qa.a: Two shared meals a week from his duty chart, a heavy curtain, and a quieter lane in the mornings for his sleep.

qa.q: How did Zubin seem to feel when he said 'I'm always sorry'?
qa.a: He seemed guilty and worn out, grey with tiredness and ashamed of missing the family lunch again.

grounding: Over a week a shift worker's wife moves from feeling neglected to planning shared meals and a quiet house for his sleep.

subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: Santosh beta, you're sulking because Meenu works nights now? Let your Jagdish Dada tell you something. In seventy-eight your Dadi took a job as a night telephone operator. I was twenty-five and proud, and I felt forgotten. I'd come home to cold rotis and a sleeping wife, and I'd bang the vessels so she would know I was upset. She woke hurt and worn out, apologising for a job we needed. One day my own father said, 'Jagdish, you are fighting her tiredness, not her.' So I learnt. I kept the house quiet till noon, took your father to the park, and we fixed Thursday evenings as ours: jalebi and a walk by the river. Forty years on, she still laughs about those vessels.

qa.q: What did young Jagdish do so his wife would know he was upset?
qa.a: He banged the vessels.

qa.q: How did young Jagdish feel when he came home to cold rotis?
qa.a: He felt forgotten and resentful, hurt that his wife's night job left him alone.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jagdish's story?
qa.a: His father saying he was fighting her tiredness, not her; after that he kept the house quiet and they fixed Thursday evenings together.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's wife feel when she woke to the banging?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worn out, apologising for a job the family needed.

grounding: A grandfather recalls feeling neglected by his wife's night shifts and learning that quiet and planned time together helped.

subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: Abhinav's birthday fell on a Wednesday, and Harish, his older brother, was on nights again at the airport cargo shed. Their one-room flat in Hyderabad had no door between the bed and the kitchen, so all day Abhinav tiptoed around a sleeping lump and ate cold lunch standing up. By evening he felt invisible. When Harish woke at six, groggy, Abhinav said flatly, "You forgot." Harish's face fell. "I didn't. I'm just... always tired. I hate missing everything." They sat on the floor. Harish pulled a slightly squashed box of mithai from his bag. Then they made a plan: Saturday breakfast together, always, whatever the rota; Abhinav would use headphones and cook after four; Harish would send the week's shifts every Sunday. It wasn't a party. But Abhinav stopped feeling like furniture.

qa.q: Where does Harish work nights?
qa.a: At the airport cargo shed.

qa.q: How was Abhinav feeling by the evening of his birthday?
qa.a: He felt invisible and neglected, having tiptoed around all day and eaten a cold lunch alone.

qa.q: Which parts of the plan help hold the relationship together?
qa.a: A fixed Saturday breakfast, quiet while Harish sleeps, and sharing the shift timetable every Sunday.

qa.q: What is it like for Harish when Abhinav says "You forgot"?
qa.a: Harish feels hurt and guilty, worn out and hating that he misses so much.

grounding: Shows a family member of a shift worker feeling neglected on a missed birthday while the worker feels guilty and worn out, and shared time, quiet for sleep and open talk holding them together.
